extraction_notes.note: The introduction's overview paragraphs are proof sketches; the sketch rule asks for rigor: semi_formal on them but rigor is not allowed on proofs, so they carry no rigor field and only alternative: true on their proves edges.

Most proofs have no proof environment and fill whole sections (Sections 3, 4, 5, 7, 8) or subsections (9.1, 9.2); each is one prose proof node with paragraph-level steps. Section 7's proof contains Lemmas 7.1 and 7.2 with their proofs.
Theorem 1.1 of [MR4510172] (Hörmander-Mikhlin singular Brascamp-Lieb bound) is only applied in Section 8 and in the overview, never stated, so it has no node.
remark or claim: the paragraph derives the symmetry identity (2.19) with its own definitions; kept as a remark containing the definitions and the equation.

nodes.name: Norm-variation bound for triple ergodic averages
nodes.statement: For all $r>4$, there exists a constant $C>0$ such that the following holds. Let $(X,\mathcal{F},\mu)$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure space, $T_0,T_1,T_2\colon~X\to X$ mutually commuting measure preserving transformations and let $J$ and $n_0<n_1<\cdots<n_J$ be positive integers. For any $f_0,f_1\in L^8(X)$ and $f_2 \in L^4(X)$, each of respective norms one, we have the bound \begin{equation*} \sum_{j=1}^{J} \|M_{n_j}(f_0,f_1,f_2) - M_{n_{j-1}}(f_0,f_1,f_2)\|_{{L}^2(X)}^r \leq C , \end{equation*} where we have defined for almost every $x\in X$ \begin{equation*} M_{n}(f_0,f_1,f_2)(x) := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} f_0(T_0^i x) f_1(T_1^i x) f_2(T_2^i x). \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: For $r>4$, the $r$-variation in $L^2$ of triple ergodic averages for three commuting measure preserving maps is uniformly bounded.
assumptions: Let $(X,\mathcal{F},\mu)$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure space
$T_0,T_1,T_2\colon~X\to X$ mutually commuting measure preserving transformations
let $J$ and $n_0<n_1<\cdots<n_J$ be positive integers
$f_0,f_1\in L^8(X)$ and $f_2 \in L^4(X)$, each of respective norms one
conclusions: there exists a constant $C>0$ such that the following holds
we have the bound \begin{equation*} \sum_{j=1}^{J} \|M_{n_j}(f_0,f_1,f_2) - M_{n_{j-1}}(f_0,f_1,f_2)\|_{{L}^2(X)}^r \leq C , \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Norm variation bounds for one and two commuting transformations
nodes.statement: Norm variation bounds with $r\ge 2$ for one transformation were proven in \cite{MR1389625} and for two commuting transformations in \cite{MR3904183}, following earlier work \cite{MR3480347} in the finite group setting.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.origin_citation: MR1389625 (one transformation); MR3904183, MR3480347 (two commuting transformations)
nodes.statement_short: Prior results: $r\ge2$ norm-variation bounds hold for one and for two commuting transformations.

nodes.name: Norm variation for any number of commuting transformations
nodes.statement: Norm variation bounds with any $r<\infty$ for any number of commuting transformations were stated as an open problem in the closing section of \cite{MR3345161}. Any such bounds remain unknown for more than three commuting transformations.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Whether norm variation bounds with some $r<\infty$ hold for any number of commuting transformations; unknown beyond three.

nodes.name: Sharp norm variation conjecture ($r\ge 2$)
nodes.statement: It is natural to conjecture norm variation bounds for $r\ge 2$ for any number of commuting transformations.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: norm variation bounds for $r\ge 2$ for any number of commuting transformations

nodes.name: Tao's norm convergence theorem
nodes.statement: Qualitative norm convergence for three or more commuting transformations was proven by Tao in \cite{MR2408398} by finitary methods.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Multiple ergodic averages for three or more commuting transformations converge in norm.

nodes.name: Birkhoff ergodic theorem
nodes.statement: Such pointwise convergence is known by the classical Birkhoff theorem for a single transformation \cite{bir30}, with pointwise variational estimates proven in \cite{MR1019960}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Pointwise convergence for two commuting transformations
nodes.statement: Pointwise convergence almost everywhere remains a widely recognized open problem even in the case of two general commuting transformations.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1 via the Calderón transference principle
nodes.statement: By a variant of the well known Calder{\'o}n transference principle, Theorem \ref{thm:ergodicthm} follows from Theorem \ref{thm:2} below. We do not elaborate on the transference principle in the present paper but refer to the case of two commuting transformations in \cite{MR3904183}. It reduces quantitative convergence results to analogous results on individual orbits of the action of the group spanned by the commuting transformations and parameterized by $\mathbb{Z}^3$. The further transfer from $\mathbb{Z}^3$ to $\mathbb{R}^3$ as in Theorem \ref{thm:2} is harmless and it can be made a part of the transference principle in our setting, unlike in the setting of actions $T^{p(n)}$ with polynomials of higher degree which face number theoretic complications.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Transference: reduce Theorem 1.1 to orbits of the $\mathbb{Z}^3$-action and then to the $\mathbb{R}^3$ statement of Theorem 1.2.

nodes.name: Apply transference principle
nodes.statement: By a variant of the well known Calder{\'o}n transference principle, Theorem \ref{thm:ergodicthm} follows from Theorem \ref{thm:2} below. We do not elaborate on the transference principle in the present paper but refer to the case of two commuting transformations in \cite{MR3904183}. It reduces quantitative convergence results to analogous results on individual orbits of the action of the group spanned by the commuting transformations and parameterized by $\mathbb{Z}^3$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Calderón transference reduces Theorem 1.1 to Theorem 1.2 on orbits of the $\mathbb{Z}^3$ action.

nodes.name: Transfer from Z^3 to R^3

nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: The passage from $\mathbb{Z}^3$ to $\mathbb{R}^3$ is harmless here.

nodes.name: Continuous norm-variation bound on R^3
nodes.statement: For all $r>4$, there exists a constant $C>0$ such that the following holds. For any positive integer $J$ and positive real numbers $t_0<t_1<\cdots < t_J$, any $f_0,f_1\in L^8({\mathbb R}^3)$ and $f_2\in {L}^4(\mathbb{R}^3)$ with respective norms one, we have \begin{equation} \sum_{j=1}^{J} \|M_{t_j}(f_0,f_1,f_2) - M_{t_{j-1}}(f_0,f_1,f_2)\|_{{L}^2({\mathbb R}^3)}^r \leq C \end{equation} where, with $e_0,e_1,e_2$ the standard unit vectors in ${\mathbb R}^3$, we have defined for almost every $x\in {\mathbb R}^3$: \begin{equation} M_{t}(f_0,f_1,f_2)(x) := \frac{1}{t}\int_0^t f_0(x+\tau e_0) f_1(x+\tau e_1) f_2(x+\tau e_2)\,d\tau. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: For $r>4$, the $r$-variation in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ of triple averages along the coordinate directions is uniformly bounded.

nodes.name: Other exponent tuples by symmetry and interpolation
nodes.statement: Only the choice of tuple of exponents $(8,8,4)$ breaks the symmetry between the three functions in the above theorems. One therefore concludes the analogous estimates for permutations of these exponents. Interpolation gives further tuples of exponents, for example the symmetric tuple $(6,6,6)$.

nodes.statement_short: By symmetry and interpolation the theorems also hold for permuted exponents and e.g. $(6,6,6)$.

nodes.name: singular Brascamp-Lieb datum
nodes.statement: A singular Brascamp-Lieb datum $D=(n,S,\Pi,(\Pi_s)_{s\in S})$ is a tuple containing the dimension $n\ge 1$ of the domain of integration, the finite set $S$ parameterizing the tuple of input functions, and linear maps $\Pi$ and $\Pi_s$ for $s\in S$ on the domain ${\mathbb R}^{n}$, where $\Pi_s$ maps onto the domain of the input function with parameter $s$, typically of smaller dimension than $n$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
differentia: containing the dimension $n\ge 1$ of the domain of integration, the finite set $S$ parameterizing the tuple of input functions, and linear maps $\Pi$ and $\Pi_s$ for $s\in S$ on the domain ${\mathbb R}^{n}$
nodes.statement_short: A datum $D=(n,S,\Pi,(\Pi_s))$: dimension, index set of functions, and linear maps from $\mathbb{R}^n$.

nodes.name: singular Brascamp-Lieb form
nodes.statement: Together with some singular integral kernel $K$ on the range of $\Pi$, the singular Brascamp-Lieb form $\Lambda_{D,K}$ is defined as \[\Lambda_{D,K}((f_s)_{s\in S})=\int_{{\mathbb R}^n} K(\Pi x)\prod_{s\in S} f_s(\Pi_sx)\, dx ,\] where the integral is defined in some principal value sense or, if the kernel has additional qualitative regularity as is mostly the case in the present paper, in the Lebesgue integral sense.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: $\Lambda_{D,K}((f_s))=\int K(\Pi x)\prod_s f_s(\Pi_s x)\,dx$ for a singular kernel $K$.

nodes.name: multiplier of the form
nodes.statement: We also often talk about the multiplier $m$ of the form, which is the Fourier transform of the kernel $K$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: singular Brascamp-Lieb inequality
nodes.statement: A singular Brascamp-Lieb inequality estimates this form by a constant times the product of Lebesgue norms $\prod_{s\in S} \|f_s\|_{p_s}$ for some tuple of exponents $p_s$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 1.2
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:2} is deduced in Section~\ref{proofthm:2} from~\eqref{eq:doublenormvar}, an estimate in terms of a fixed number $J$ of jumps in the variation, which can be thought of as an endpoint estimate at $r=4$ for~\eqref{e:main2}. This endpoint estimate is reduced to two singular Brascamp-Lieb estimates, both with datum $D_1$ defined in \eqref{defd1}, but with different two-dimensional kernels illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:1}. For simplicity we focus on one quadrant in our discussion, as the other quadrants do not pose additional difficulties. The first singular Brascamp-Lieb estimate, Proposition \ref{prop:1}, takes care of the so-called short variation with a multiplier that lives near the dark blue overlap regions of the light blue squares in Figure \ref{fig:1}. The size of each dark blue square is comparable to its distance to the origin, a property we call Whitney. Proposition \ref{prop:2} takes care of the so-called long variation with multipliers living at the light blue squares themselves. Each light blue square includes potentially many scales and therefore is not in general Whitney. However, the piece of the multiplier associated with each light blue square has elementary tensor structure and telescopes into the difference between its largest and its smallest scale. For both of these propositions, it is important that the number of squares involved is controlled by $J$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: reduce to the $r=4$ endpoint, then to short (Prop. 2.1) and long (Prop. 2.3) variation Brascamp-Lieb estimates.

nodes.name: Whitney (property of a frequency square)

nodes.name: Reduce to endpoint and two BL estimates
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:2} is deduced in Section~\ref{proofthm:2} from~\eqref{eq:doublenormvar}, an estimate in terms of a fixed number $J$ of jumps in the variation, which can be thought of as an endpoint estimate at $r=4$ for~\eqref{e:main2}. This endpoint estimate is reduced to two singular Brascamp-Lieb estimates, both with datum $D_1$ defined in \eqref{defd1}, but with different two-dimensional kernels illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:1}. nodes.statement_short: Theorem 1.2 follows from the $r=4$ endpoint estimate, reduced to two Brascamp-Lieb estimates with datum $D_1$.

nodes.name: Short variation via Proposition 2.1
nodes.statement: The first singular Brascamp-Lieb estimate, Proposition \ref{prop:1}, takes care of the so-called short variation with a multiplier that lives near the dark blue overlap regions of the light blue squares in Figure \ref{fig:1}. The size of each dark blue square is comparable to its distance to the origin, a property we call Whitney.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Short variation uses Whitney multipliers handled by Proposition 2.1.

nodes.name: Long variation via Proposition 2.3
nodes.statement: Proposition \ref{prop:2} takes care of the so-called long variation with multipliers living at the light blue squares themselves. Each light blue square includes potentially many scales and therefore is not in general Whitney. However, the piece of the multiplier associated with each light blue square has elementary tensor structure and telescopes into the difference between its largest and its smallest scale. For both of these propositions, it is important that the number of squares involved is controlled by $J$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Long variation uses telescoping tensor multipliers handled by Proposition 2.3.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Proposition 2.3
nodes.statement: Proposition \ref{prop:2} is proved in Section \ref{sec:prop:2}. Multipliers vanishing on the diagonal in Figure \ref{fig:1} play a role as auxiliary objects. We use a positivity of multipliers symmetric across the diagonal to pass to a similar multiplier $m_1$ associated with light blue squares but constant on the diagonal. We then define two further multipliers $m_2$ and $m_3$ so that $m_1+m_2+m_3$ is constant in the entire plane. This constant multiplier allows a trivial bound, reducing the estimate for $m_1$ to estimates for $m_2$ and $m_3$. Multiplier $m_2$ is addressed in Proposition \ref{firststick}. It is supported near the red sticks in Figure \ref{fig:1}. Each stick is away from the diagonal and has possibly many scales and is therefore not in general Whitney. However, the multiplier associated with each stick is an elementary tensor and as such telescopes into a small number of scales. The multiplier $m_1+m_2$ is constant both on the diagonal as well as on the white L-shaped regions in Figure \ref{fig:cones}. The multiplier $m_3$ is addressed in Proposition \ref{firstcz}. It is supported in the at most $J$ purple regions in between the white L- shaped regions and vanishes on the diagonal. Each purple region has a single scale and is Whitney. We decompose $m_3$ into a lacunary family of cones towards the diagonal shown in Figure \ref{fig:cones}. Each lacunary piece is estimated with Lemma 3 in \cite{MR4171366}. Thanks to vanishing on the diagonal, one has a geometric sum for the estimates in this family.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: by positivity pass to $m_1$, complete it to a constant with $m_2$ (Prop. 2.6) and $m_3$ (Prop. 2.5).

nodes.name: Complete multiplier to a constant
nodes.statement: Proposition \ref{prop:2} is proved in Section \ref{sec:prop:2}. Multipliers vanishing on the diagonal in Figure \ref{fig:1} play a role as auxiliary objects. We use a positivity of multipliers symmetric across the diagonal to pass to a similar multiplier $m_1$ associated with light blue squares but constant on the diagonal. We then define two further multipliers $m_2$ and $m_3$ so that $m_1+m_2+m_3$ is constant in the entire plane. This constant multiplier allows a trivial bound, reducing the estimate for $m_1$ to estimates for $m_2$ and $m_3$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Use positivity to pass to $m_1$ and add $m_2,m_3$ so the sum is constant.

nodes.name: Stick multiplier m_2
nodes.statement: Multiplier $m_2$ is addressed in Proposition \ref{firststick}. It is supported near the red sticks in Figure \ref{fig:1}. Each stick is away from the diagonal and has possibly many scales and is therefore not in general Whitney. However, the multiplier associated with each stick is an elementary tensor and as such telescopes into a small number of scales.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: $m_2$ lives near off-diagonal sticks and is handled by Proposition 2.6.

nodes.name: Cone multiplier m_3
nodes.statement: The multiplier $m_1+m_2$ is constant both on the diagonal as well as on the white L-shaped regions in Figure \ref{fig:cones}. The multiplier $m_3$ is addressed in Proposition \ref{firstcz}. It is supported in the at most $J$ purple regions in between the white L- shaped regions and vanishes on the diagonal. Each purple region has a single scale and is Whitney. We decompose $m_3$ into a lacunary family of cones towards the diagonal shown in Figure \ref{fig:cones}. Each lacunary piece is estimated with Lemma 3 in \cite{MR4171366}. Thanks to vanishing on the diagonal, one has a geometric sum for the estimates in this family.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: $m_3$ is decomposed into lacunary cones, each bounded by Lemma 3 of [DT], summing geometrically.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Proposition 2.1
nodes.statement: Proposition \ref{prop:1} is proved in Section \ref{sec:prop:1}. We combine the dark blue squares with a suitable family of light blue squares with tensor structure to obtain a multiplier vanishing on the diagonal. The light blue squares are estimated with Proposition \ref{prop:2}, while the multiplier vanishing on the diagonal is estimated with Proposition \ref{firstcz}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: add tensor squares to vanish on the diagonal; bound them by Prop. 2.3 and the rest by Prop. 2.5.

nodes.name: Combine with tensor squares
nodes.statement: Proposition \ref{prop:1} is proved in Section \ref{sec:prop:1}. We combine the dark blue squares with a suitable family of light blue squares with tensor structure to obtain a multiplier vanishing on the diagonal.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Combine Whitney squares with tensor-structured squares to get a multiplier vanishing on the diagonal.

nodes.name: Apply Propositions 2.3 and 2.5
nodes.statement: The light blue squares are estimated with Proposition \ref{prop:2}, while the multiplier vanishing on the diagonal is estimated with Proposition \ref{firstcz}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Estimate the pieces by Propositions 2.3 and 2.5.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Proposition 2.6
nodes.statement: Proposition \ref{firststick} is proved in Section \ref{sec:firststick}. Using the off-diagonal property of the multiplier to preserve crucial cancellation in the innermost integral, we apply the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in the remaining integrals. We estimate one of the factors on the right-hand side of Cauchy-Schwarz using that the multiplier has $J$ summands, which leads to the loss of $J^{\frac 12}$. The other factor we estimate loss-free thanks to the above mentioned cancellation. This loss-free estimate takes the form of a singular Brascamp-Lieb form with datum $D_2$ defined in \eqref{defd2}. The multiplier $m$ is now three-dimensional, but consisting of pieces that are naturally of the form \begin{equation} \phi_1(\theta \cdot v_1) \phi_2(\theta \cdot v_2) \end{equation} with two vectors $v_1=(0,0,1)$ and $v_2=(1,-1,0)$ as shown in Figure \ref{3dfigure}. \begin{figure} \centering \includegraphics{figure3.pdf} \caption{Three-dimensional multiplier} \end{figure} Typical behaviour of the functions $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ is shown in Figure \ref{3dfigure} on the planes perpendicular to $v_1$ and $v_2$. An important role is played by multipliers vanishing on the critical space spanned by $v_1$ and $v_2$. Such multipliers are estimated in Propositions \ref{secstickphi} and \ref{secstickgauss} in the non-Whitney case and by Theorem 1.1 in~\cite{MR4510172} in the Whitney case. The multiplier $m$ does not vanish on the critical space. It is first modified using Proposition \ref{secstickphi} towards a multiplier $m'$ that also consists of pieces as in \eqref{2d3d} but is more symmetric in the variables $\xi,\eta$. The multiplier $m'$ is then estimated by Proposition \ref{thm:4}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: Cauchy-Schwarz with a $J^{1/2}$ loss on one factor; the other is a loss-free $D_2$ form handled by Props. 2.8 and 2.7.

nodes.name: Cauchy-Schwarz preserving cancellation
nodes.statement: Proposition \ref{firststick} is proved in Section \ref{sec:firststick}. Using the off-diagonal property of the multiplier to preserve crucial cancellation in the innermost integral, we apply the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in the remaining integrals.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Keep the innermost cancellation and apply Cauchy-Schwarz in the remaining integrals.

nodes.name: Estimate the two factors
nodes.statement: We estimate one of the factors on the right-hand side of Cauchy-Schwarz using that the multiplier has $J$ summands, which leads to the loss of $J^{\frac 12}$. The other factor we estimate loss-free thanks to the above mentioned cancellation. This loss-free estimate takes the form of a singular Brascamp-Lieb form with datum $D_2$ defined in \eqref{defd2}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: One factor loses $J^{1/2}$; the other is a loss-free form with datum $D_2$.

nodes.name: Structure of the 3D multiplier
nodes.statement: The multiplier $m$ is now three-dimensional, but consisting of pieces that are naturally of the form \begin{equation} \phi_1(\theta \cdot v_1) \phi_2(\theta \cdot v_2) \end{equation} with two vectors $v_1=(0,0,1)$ and $v_2=(1,-1,0)$ as shown in Figure \ref{3dfigure}. \begin{figure} \centering \includegraphics{figure3.pdf} \caption{Three-dimensional multiplier} \end{figure} Typical behaviour of the functions $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ is shown in Figure \ref{3dfigure} on the planes perpendicular to $v_1$ and $v_2$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: The 3D multiplier consists of pieces of the form (1.3).

nodes.name: Modify and apply Proposition 2.7
nodes.statement: An important role is played by multipliers vanishing on the critical space spanned by $v_1$ and $v_2$. Such multipliers are estimated in Propositions \ref{secstickphi} and \ref{secstickgauss} in the non-Whitney case and by Theorem 1.1 in~\cite{MR4510172} in the Whitney case. The multiplier $m$ does not vanish on the critical space. It is first modified using Proposition \ref{secstickphi} towards a multiplier $m'$ that also consists of pieces as in \eqref{2d3d} but is more symmetric in the variables $\xi,\eta$. The multiplier $m'$ is then estimated by Proposition \ref{thm:4}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Two-dimensional flavored pieces (1.3)
nodes.statement: \phi_1(\theta \cdot v_1) \phi_2(\theta \cdot v_2)
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.label: 2d3d

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Proposition 2.7
nodes.statement: Proposition \ref{thm:4} is proved in Section \ref{sec:thm:4}. The key to estimating non-Whitney multipliers such as $m'$ is a new variant of a telescoping identity in this context that concerns three-dimensional multipliers with a two dimensional flavor as in Figure \ref{3dfigure} and \eqref{2d3d}. This identity telescopes a trivial multiplier, the product of the lightest blue squares minus the product of the darkest blue squares, into two sums consisting of products of a square in one plane with a difference of the corresponding square with a consecutive square in the other plane. One sum is arranged to allow a positivity argument using reflection symmetry across the diagonal in the $\xi,\eta$ plane, the other sum is arranged similarly to allow a positivity argument with symmetry in the shown skew coordinates in the other plane. As the two positive sums add to a trivial multiplier, both are individually bounded. The given multiplier $m'$ can be dominated by one of these constructed multipliers, using various modifications with Propositions \ref{secstickphi} and \ref{secstickgauss} and Theorem 1.1 in~\cite{MR4510172}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: a telescoping identity splits a trivial multiplier into two positive sums; $m'$ is dominated by one of them.

nodes.name: Telescoping identity
nodes.statement: Proposition \ref{thm:4} is proved in Section \ref{sec:thm:4}. The key to estimating non-Whitney multipliers such as $m'$ is a new variant of a telescoping identity in this context that concerns three-dimensional multipliers with a two dimensional flavor as in Figure \ref{3dfigure} and \eqref{2d3d}. This identity telescopes a trivial multiplier, the product of the lightest blue squares minus the product of the darkest blue squares, into two sums consisting of products of a square in one plane with a difference of the corresponding square with a consecutive square in the other plane.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: A new telescoping identity splits a trivial multiplier into two sums.

nodes.name: Positivity by reflection symmetry
nodes.statement: One sum is arranged to allow a positivity argument using reflection symmetry across the diagonal in the $\xi,\eta$ plane, the other sum is arranged similarly to allow a positivity argument with symmetry in the shown skew coordinates in the other plane. As the two positive sums add to a trivial multiplier, both are individually bounded.

nodes.statement_short: Each sum is positive by a symmetry, so both are bounded.

nodes.name: Dominate m'
nodes.statement: The given multiplier $m'$ can be dominated by one of these constructed multipliers, using various modifications with Propositions \ref{secstickphi} and \ref{secstickgauss} and Theorem 1.1 in~\cite{MR4510172}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Dominate $m'$ by one of these using Propositions 2.8, 2.9 and Theorem 1.1 of [DST].

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Propositions 2.8 and 2.9
nodes.statement: Propositions \ref{secstickphi} and \ref{secstickgauss} are proved in Section \ref{sec:secstick}. Vanishing of the multiplier on the critical space allows a lacunary decomposition away from the critical space and a further Cauchy-Schwarz. This leads to singular Brascamp-Lieb estimates with a standard cubical datum and three-fold telescoping identities for three-dimensional kernels. The non-Whitney property requires telescoping along the scales of the variation sequences. There is a mix of discrete telescoping and partial integration, with \ref{secstickphi} more discrete and \ref{secstickgauss} more continuous. Analogous but simpler techniques appear in the Whitney case in Theorem 1.1 in~\cite{MR4510172}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: lacunary decomposition away from the critical space, Cauchy-Schwarz, then cubical BL forms with three-fold telescoping.

nodes.name: Lacunary decomposition and Cauchy-Schwarz
nodes.statement: Propositions \ref{secstickphi} and \ref{secstickgauss} are proved in Section \ref{sec:secstick}. Vanishing of the multiplier on the critical space allows a lacunary decomposition away from the critical space and a further Cauchy-Schwarz.

nodes.name: Cubical datum and telescoping

nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: This yields cubical Brascamp-Lieb forms with three-fold telescoping identities along the scales.

nodes.name: Discrete vs continuous telescoping
nodes.statement: There is a mix of discrete telescoping and partial integration, with \ref{secstickphi} more discrete and \ref{secstickgauss} more continuous. Analogous but simpler techniques appear in the Whitney case in Theorem 1.1 in~\cite{MR4510172}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 2.8 telescopes discretely, 2.9 more continuously.

nodes.name: datum $D_1$
nodes.statement: Put coordinates \[x=(x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3^0,x_3^1)\] on ${\mathbb R}^5$. Define \begin{equation} D_1:=(5,S, \Pi,(\Pi_s)_{s\in S}) \end{equation} with $S=\{0,1,2\}\times \{0,1\}$, with $\Pi$ mapping ${\mathbb R}^5$ to ${\mathbb R}^2$ as \[\Pi(x)=(x_3^0-x_0-x_1-x_2, x_3^1-x_0-x_1-x_2),\] and with $\Pi_s$ for $s=(k,j)$ mapping ${\mathbb R}^5$ to ${\mathbb R}^3$ as \[\Pi_{(k,j)}(x)=(x_0,x_1,x_2)-x_ke_k+ x_3^j e_k.\]

nodes.name: singular Brascamp-Lieb estimate (2.2) for $D_1$
nodes.statement: Each of the three following propositions will have a constant $C$, a parameter $J$ and formulate a class of kernels $K$ such that the singular Brascamp-Lieb estimate \begin{equation} |\Lambda_{D_1,K} ((f_s)_{s\in S})|\le CJ^{\frac 12} \end{equation} holds for all tuples of real-valued Schwartz functions $(f_{s})_{s\in S}$ such that \begin{equation} f_{(k,0)}=f_{(k,1)} \end{equation} for each $k\in \{0,1,2\}$ and \begin{equation} \|f_{(0,j)}\|_{8}=\|f_{(1,j)}\|_{8} =\|f_{(2,j)}\|_{4} =1 \end{equation} for each $j\in \{0,1\}$.

nodes.name: Role of the parameter lambda and constants
nodes.statement: We note that the particular value $\lambda=\frac{3}{2}$ is not essential for the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:1}. Evidently, the analogous statement of the proposition becomes stronger for smaller values of $\lambda$. Our proof can be pushed to $\lambda>1$ at the expense of allowing the constant in~\eqref{lambdabd} to depend on $\lambda$. On the other hand, the upper bound $\lambda<2$ is needed to apply Proposition~\ref{prop:1} to prove Theorem~\ref{thm:2}. nodes.name: Hidden symmetry of the datum D_2
nodes.statement: We remark on a symmetry in the datum $D_2$. We do a change of variables in the kernel using the linear map \[L(a,b,c)= (a+b-c, a-b,c).\] Define \[\widetilde{\Pi}(x):=L\circ \Pi(x)= (x_2^{0}+x_2^{1}-x_3^{0}-x_3^1-2(x_0+x_1), x_2^0-x_2^1, x_3^1-x_3^0).\] Define $\widetilde{D}_2$ from $D_2$ by replacing $\Pi$ by $\widetilde{\Pi}$ and choose $\widetilde{K}$ so that $\widetilde{K}\circ L=K$. We obtain $$\Lambda_{D_2,K}((f_s)_{s\in S})=\Lambda_{\widetilde{D}_2,\widetilde{K}}(({f}_s)_{s\in S}).$$ The map $\widetilde{\Pi}$ has a symmetry under interchanging the last two entries at the same time as precomposing with the involution $$(x_0,x_1,x_2^{0},x_3^{0},x_2^{1},x_3^{1})\mapsto (x_0,x_1,-x_3^{0},-x_2^{0},-x_3^{1},-x_2^{1})$$ This involution can be seen as acting on the tuple of functions $f_s$, and hence we have the following consequence for the associated form. Define $\widetilde{K}^*(a,b,c)=\widetilde{K}(a,c,b)$. For $j\in \mathcal{C}$, define $j^*\in \mathcal{C}$ by $j^*(l)=j(1-l)$ and define $f^*_{(k,j)}(a,b,c)=f_{(k,j^*)}(a,-c,-b)$. Then \begin{equation} \Lambda_{\widetilde{D}_2,\widetilde{K}}(({f}_s)_{s\in S}) =\Lambda_{\widetilde{D}_2,\widetilde{K}^*}(({f}_s^*)_{s\in S}). \end{equation}

We put coordinates $x=(x_1^0,x_2^0,x_{3}^0,x_{1}^1,x_{2}^1,x_{3}^1)$ on ${\mathbb R}^6$. We define \begin{equation} D_A:=(6,S, \Pi,(\Pi_s)_{s\in S}), \end{equation} where the projection $\Pi:{\mathbb R}^6\to {\mathbb R}^3$ is given by \begin{equation} \Pi(x)^T = (I,A) x^T, \end{equation} where $I$ is the $3\times 3$ identity matrix and $(I,A)$ is a $3 \times 6$ block matrix. nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.10
nodes.statement: Let $\psi :[0,\infty) \to {\mathbb R}$ be a smooth monotone decreasing function with \[\psi(x)=1/2 \ \ {\rm for}\ \ x\in [0, 5/6],\] \[\psi(x)=0 \ \ {\rm for}\ \ x\in [1, \infty).\] Let $\rho:[0,\infty) \to {\mathbb R}$ be a smooth monotone increasing function with \[\rho(x)=0 \ \ {\rm for}\ \ x\in [0, 1/2],\] \[\rho(x)=3^{1/2} \ \ {\rm for}\ \ x\in [4/6, \infty).\] There exists a smooth even function $\phi_0$ on ${\mathbb R}$ such that its Fourier transform is nonnegative and satisfies on $[0,\infty)$ \begin{equation*} (\widehat{\phi_0})^2= (4-\rho^2)\psi^2,\end{equation*} because the right-hand side equals $\psi^2$ on $[4/6,\infty)$ and is bounded below by $1/4$ on $[0,5/6]$ and constant one on $[0,1/2)$. There exists a smooth even function $\phi_1$ on ${\mathbb R}$ such that its Fourier transform is nonnegative and fulfills on the interval $[0,\infty)$ \begin{equation*} (1-\widehat{\phi_1})^2=1-(4 -\rho^2)\psi^2,\end{equation*} because the right-hand side equals $\rho^2/4$ on $[0,5/6]$ and is bounded below by $3/4$ on $[4/6,\infty)$ and constant on $[0,1/2]$. The pair $(\phi_0,\phi_1)$ then satisfies the assumptions for a $c$-pair with $$c=\max(\|{\widehat{\phi_0}}^{(N+30)}\|_\infty, \|{\widehat{\phi_1}}^{(N+30)}\|_\infty).$$ This proves the lemma.
